content: Salbutamol, also known as albuterol in the United States, is a short-acting β2-adrenergic receptor agonist. It is primarily used to relieve bronchospasm in conditions such as asthma and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD). Salbutamol sulfate is most commonly administered via inhalation to directly target bronchial smooth muscle. Delivery methods include devices like Rotahalers or Autohalers. When inhaled, the maximal effect of salbutamol typically occurs within 5 to 20 minutes, although some relief can be observed almost immediately. Salbutamol can also be administered orally or intravenously, but certain individuals with asthma may not respond to the medication due to the absence of a specific DNA base sequence in a particular gene. Salbutamol was first introduced in the United Kingdom in 1969 and became available in the United States in 1980 under the trade name Ventolin. Clinical Use Salbutamol is specifically indicated for the following conditions: Acute asthma attacks. Symptom relief during maintenance therapy for asthma and other conditions involving reversible airway obstruction, including COPD. Prevention of exercise-induced asthma. Management of hyperkalemia, particularly in patients with renal failure. Aerosolized administration via a nebulizer for patients with cystic fibrosis, often in combination with ipratropium bromide and dornase alfa (Pulmozyme). As a β2-agonist, salbutamol is also used in obstetrics. Intravenous salbutamol can act as a tocolytic agent, relaxing uterine smooth muscle to delay premature labor. However, its use in this context has largely been replaced by nifedipine, a calcium-channel blocker that is more effective, better tolerated, and can be administered orally. Mode of Action Salbutamol, like other β2-adrenergic receptor agonists, binds preferentially to β2-adrenergic receptors over β1-receptors. In the airways, activation of β2-receptors leads to relaxation of bronchial smooth muscle, resulting in bronchodilation and widening of the airways. Inhaled salbutamol sulfate has a rapid onset of action, providing relief within 5 to 15 minutes of administration. In the context of tocolysis, activation of β2-receptors relaxes uterine smooth muscle, thereby delaying labor. Adverse Effects Salbutamol is generally well-tolerated, especially when compared to older therapies like theophylline. However, adverse drug reactions can occur, particularly at high doses or when administered orally or intravenously. Common side effects include tremor, palpitations, and headache. Less common side effects include tachycardia, muscle cramps, agitation, hypokalemia, tinnitus, hyperactivity in children, and insomnia. The (S)-enantiomer of salbutamol may inhibit the anti-inflammatory effects of steroids prescribed for asthma treatment, while the (R)-enantiomer enhances the steroid's effect. The overall interaction between the two enantiomers remains unclear. Other Brand Names Salbutamol is marketed under various brand names, including Aerolin, Airomir, Asthalin, Asthavent, Asmol, Buventol, ProAir, Proventil, Salamol, Sultanol, Ventolin, and Volmax. The (R)-enantiomer of salbutamol, known as levalbuterol, is sold under the brand name Xopenex. In the United States, regulators announced a ban on albuterol inhalers containing chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs) starting in 2009. Previously, these inhalers were exempt from the national CFC-production ban due to their essential use status. Manufacturers were expected to produce sufficient supplies of alternative inhalers by 2009 and offer discounts for patients unable to afford the newer versions, which cost approximately $20 more. Interestingly, CFC-free inhalers have been available in the United Kingdom for several years, raising questions about the pricing disparity.
